title: Redwood discovery with Stratus Capital
summary: Intro discovery focused on unit economics: per-token pricing, batching and caching levers, and suitability of Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for a hedge fund inference workload. Customer has strict budget targets and latency requirements for real-time signals; wants benchmark pilot and security docs.
topics: Dedicated reserved capacity and commit economics
action_items: Alex Chen | Send hosted vs dedicated pricing spreadsheet + sample unit economics for 200M tokens/day | 2026-03-18
Priya Shah | Propose benchmark workload and test plan (latency + batch sizes) | 2026-03-20
Tom Evans | Share current token/sec metrics and peak concurrency examples | 2026-03-17
next_steps: Redwood to send pricing sheet and quantization/batching guidance
Schedule 2-hour technical benchmark session week of 2026-03-23 with Stratus infra and ML
Customer to share sample request distribution and SLO targets
transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, from Redwood, I'm Alex Chen AE and Priya is our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:06] Michael: Good, thanks. Michael here. Uh, we've been looking at Redwood compared to other providers, mostly from a unit cost standpoint.
[00:12] Priya: Awesome, thanks. Do you want to start with a quick agenda? We'll focus on latency SLOs, expected volumes, and then dig into pricing and batching options.
[00:20] Sara: Yeah that works. Our main problem: we're doing real-time signals for trading strategies, so we need per-request 200-400ms p50 ideally, and cost has to be under a hard budget, we're targeting something like $X per million tokens, long story short.
[00:34] Alex: Cool. Can you share current traffic? bursts, average tokens per request?
[00:39] Tom: Typical request is ~120 tokens input, 80 tokens generation, but we get spikes during market opens to ~350 concurrent requests. Average daily tokens ~200M.
[00:47] Priya: That's helpful. So quick framing: Hosted gives you fastest onboarding and per-token pricing. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and lower per-token unit costs at scale — especially when you use batching and KV caching. Private is for VPC/on-prem when you need full network isolation, more ops but fixed costs.
[01:05] Michael: Ok, quantify "lower per-token" — like how much can we expect to save if we go dedicated vs hosted?
[01:09] Priya: Sure. Roughly speaking, on Hosted we have a baseline list price for generation tokens, let's call it $0.03 per 1k tokens for a mid-size model — this is ballpark, not final. Dedicated can drop the net unit cost 20–40% after reserved capacity and effective batching. With aggressive batching and prefix/KV caching you sometimes see effective per-token compute down another 10–15% because you amortize kernel launch and attention costs.
[01:29] Michael: That range is wide. We need a worked example. Could you run through one for our 200M tokens/day?
[01:34] Alex: Absolutely. Example scenario: 200M tokens/day -> ~6B tokens/month. If hosted list is $0.03/1k, that's $180k/month compute. On Dedicated with a 12-month commit we might reduce to $0.02/1k effective which is $120k/month, plus reserved infra fee, so net maybe $130k after amortized infra, so roughly 25% savings. If you add caching — say 10% of tokens are prefix hits — you get another effective reduction.
[02:03] Sara: How do you estimate the caching hit rate? Our requests have a lot of overlap due to repeated prompts.
[02:08] Priya: We typically instrument a small sample. Prefix caching for repeated prompts often yields 5–20% token savings depending on how templated requests are. KV cache helps for multi-turn sessions; for stateless single-turn repeated prompts prefix caching is the biggest win.
[02:23] Tom: What's the batching tradeoff? We can't add 100ms in tail latency.
[02:27] Priya: Right. We operate continuous batching with latency-aware thresholds. For your 200–400ms p50 target, we can use small micro-batches and prioritization. The biggest wins come from larger tokens per request and higher concurrency. At your peak, batching will be aggressive and reduce per-token CPU/GPU setup overhead; at low volume, batching has little effect.
[02:44] Michael: So do you have numbers for p50/p95 at different batch sizes?
[02:48] Priya: Rough ballpark: for a 16-token generation with a mid-size model on a particular GPU, single-request latency might be 80ms, batching to 8 requests might produce 120–150ms, but throughput increases, so per-token cost falls. For your 120-in / 80-out example, micro-batches of 2–4 keep p50 near your target. We'll test exact model/quantization combos.
[03:08] Michael: Quantization — does Redwood support 4-bit / 8-bit?
[03:11] Priya: Yes; we support quantized variants and recommend different profiles per workload. Quantization reduces memory and sometimes inference cost per token, but can affect quality for some models; we have quality metrics to evaluate.
[03:21] Sara: For our trading models, small hallucinations are a no-go; we need to keep quality tight. How do you measure quality regression when moving to quantized or smaller models?
[03:28] Priya: We tie quality monitoring to eval suites and prompt sets. For a pilot we run AB comparisons, measure logits, and domain-specific metrics. We'll include regression thresholds in the pilot plan.
[03:36] Alex: Back to economics: another lever is smart routing — you can route non-latency-critical requests to cheaper regions, or to cheaper model variants. That often reduces average unit cost without impacting critical SLOs.
[03:45] Michael: What's the delta on routing? If we route 30% of work to cheaper endpoints, how does that show up?
[03:49] Priya: If 30% is routed to a cheaper model or region with half the price, net blended rate reduces accordingly. We'll model blended unit economics in the pricing sheet.
[03:57] Tom: We have security concerns — KMS, audit logs, SOC2. If we go Hosted, is our data seen by Redwood?
[04:03] Alex: Hosted keeps data encrypted in transit and at rest; we offer SOC 2 and encryption; we also have options for masking and dedicated instances with customer-managed keys for Dedicated or Private. For the highest security we can do Private with customer KMS and on-prem packages. We'll include the security docs.
[04:20] Michael: Good. I want the numbers again with committed capacity. If we commit to 12-months, what's the upfront vs monthly and how do we model overage?
[04:28] Priya: Typically we structure a reserved capacity commit: an agreed monthly throughput and discounted unit price. Overage is charged at a higher rate but you can configure burst capacity. We'll model commitments vs expected utilization to show net cost. Example: commit to 80% of your peak capacity, get 30% discount; bursts billed at a premium or routed to hosted.
[04:47] Sara: For our procurement, we need line-item costs: compute, infra reservation, storage, observability add-ons. Can you break those out?
[04:54] Alex: Yes, the pricing sheet will separate compute per-token, reserved infra fee, monitoring retention add-ons, and premium SLA. We'll send a sample spreadsheet.
[05:01] Tom: For benchmarking, we want to reproduce our request distribution. Do you run microbenchmarks on-prem?
[05:06] Priya: We'll run a benchmark in our dedicated environment or a private cluster depending on the chosen path. For hosted we can run against a staging endpoint. We'll need a representative workload, sample prompts, and desired SLOs.
[05:17] Michael: What about deployment time? If we pick Dedicated, how long to stand up?
[05:21] Alex: From contract signature, Dedicated typically takes 4–8 weeks depending on network and infra requirements. Private on-prem can take longer due to procurement. Hosted is immediate.
[05:30] Sara: Our security team will want SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs — do you support that?
[05:35] Priya: Yes for Enterprise: SSO, RBAC, fine-grained audit logs, and integrations with customer KMS. We'll include those in the security pack.
[05:44] Michael: Ok, let's get into a granular worked example — Alex, can you talk numbers with assumptions?
[05:48] Alex: Sure. Assumptions: 200M tokens/day, 6B tokens/month. Hosted list price $0.03/1k tokens -> compute $180k/mo. Dedicated committed price $0.02/1k -> $120k/mo compute. Add reserved infra amortized $10k/mo -> $130k. Add observability and retention -> +$5k. Net hosted vs dedicated -> $185k vs $135k, savings ~$50k/mo. With caching and routing assume another 10% effective token reduction -> dedicated could look like $121k/mo.
[06:20] Tom: That looks promising. For the pilot can we test both hosted and dedicated to verify?
[06:25] Priya: We usually run a benchmark: start hosted to confirm functional and latency, then a dedicated pilot with a small reserved pool to validate throughput and cost. We'll do side-by-side run and produce logs and cost modeling.
[06:35] Sara: What about pricing for embeddings? We also do embeddings at scale for similarity search, about 50M embeddings/month.
[06:41] Alex: Embeddings are usually priced separately per unit. We'll include embedding unit economics in the sheet; dedicated can also save on embeddings when colocated.
[06:49] Michael: Any hidden costs we should plan for? Networking, egress, storage?
[06:54] Priya: Egress and storage both can add up. For Private on-prem, you pay infra; for Hosted, egress tiers may apply. We'll call out these line items.
[07:03] Tom: Our legal will need contract language around data residency and breach responsibilities.
[07:07] Alex: Noted — we'll loop in legal and share standard terms; custom clauses can be discussed during contracting.
[07:13] Michael: Ok, next steps?
[07:15] Alex: We'll send a pricing spreadsheet with the worked examples, security pack, and a proposed benchmark plan. Priya will propose the test plan and we'll schedule a 2-hour deep benchmark session for week of 3/23.
[07:25] Sara: Sounds good.
[07:27] Michael: One question — when you say 20–40% savings on Dedicated, is that typical for model types like Llama variants?
[07:33] Priya: For open Llama-like models, Dedicated often shows bigger margins because the runtime and kernel selection is tuned; combined with quantization you can hit the higher end. For larger proprietary models the delta is smaller. We'll test with your target models.
[07:46] Tom: Also what's the expected ops involvement for Private vs Dedicated?
[07:50] Alex: Dedicated is managed by Redwood but you get reserved capacity; ops is minimal from your side for hosted and dedicated. Private requires more involvement from your infra team for networking and KMS but we provide an installer and runbook.
[07:59] Michael: Great. Any blockers we should know now?
[08:03] Priya: Just need sample prompts and a short spike dataset; Tom mentioned we'll get metrics. Once we have those, we can size and propose commit levels.
[08:12] Tom: I'll send our token/sec during peak, plus a sample of 2k requests.
[08:17] Alex: Perfect. We'll also include recommended batching and quantization profiles and a sample cost model with sensitivity to caching rates and routing mix.
[08:27] Sara: And the pilot timeline?
[08:29] Priya: Proposed: benchmark design by 3/20, benchmark session 3/23–3/27, initial results within the week.
[08:36] Michael: That's acceptable. Let's recap action items.
[08:39] Alex: Alex to send pricing sheet and security docs by 3/18. Priya to send benchmark plan by 3/20. Tom to send sample traffic and peak metrics by 3/17.
[08:48] Sara: Thanks everyone.
[08:50] Michael: Thanks.
[08:52] Alex: Thanks all. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the tech session.
[47:30] [call end — recording stops abruptly, some background noise at the end]
notes: Customer is price-sensitive and latency-sensitive; favors pilot to validate unit economics
SE recommended staged approach: hosted quick validation -> dedicated pilot -> private if required by compliance
